adverse benefit determination: The formal name for a denial: any decision by your plan to refuse, reduce, or stop paying for care.
allowed amount: The most your plan will pay for a service. Anything the provider charges above this is either written off (in network) or may be billed to you (out of network).
appeal: A formal request asking your plan to change its decision. The first one goes to the plan itself (internal appeal).
balance billing: When an out-of-network provider bills you for the difference between what they charged and what your plan paid. The No Surprises Act bans this in emergencies and at in-network facilities.
claim: A bill your provider sends to your plan asking to be paid for a service.
claim file: Everything the plan looked at when deciding your claim: records, notes, the criteria used, and the reviewer's conclusions. You can get it for free.
clinical criteria: The written medical rules or guidelines a plan uses to decide whether care is necessary. You have the right to see the ones used for your claim.
coinsurance: Your share of the cost of a service, as a percentage (for example, 20%), after you meet your deductible.
copay: A fixed amount (for example, $30) you pay for a service.
deductible: The amount you pay for covered care each year before your plan starts paying.
EOB: Explanation of Benefits: a statement from your plan showing what a provider charged, what the plan paid, and what you may owe. It is not a bill.
ERISA: The federal law that governs most job-based benefit plans. It sets the minimum appeal rules for those plans.
expedited review: A faster appeal (decided within 72 hours) for situations where waiting could seriously harm your health.
experimental or investigational: A plan's label for treatment it considers not yet proven. Denials on this basis can usually be reviewed by an outside expert.
external review: A review of your denial by an independent organization that your plan does not control. Available after the internal appeal, or at the same time if urgent.
final adverse determination: The plan's last word after your internal appeal. It starts the clock for external review.
fully insured: A plan where an insurance company takes on the risk and pays claims. State insurance laws apply to it.
grievance: California's word for a complaint or appeal filed with your health plan.
IMR: Independent Medical Review: California's free outside review of medical-necessity and similar denials, run through the state regulator.
in network: Providers that have a contract with your plan. You pay less when you use them.
internal appeal: Your first appeal, decided by the plan itself. You have at least 180 days to file it.
IRO: Independent Review Organization: an outside company certified to review denials. Texas uses this term for its external review.
medical necessity: A plan's judgment about whether care was needed and appropriate. It is the most common reason for denials, and one of the most often overturned.
member ID: The number on your insurance card that identifies you to the plan.
out of network: Providers without a contract with your plan. Your costs are usually higher, unless a surprise-billing protection applies.
out-of-pocket maximum: The most you have to pay for covered care in a year. After that, the plan pays 100%.
peer-to-peer review: A phone call between your doctor and the plan's medical reviewer to discuss the denial. Doctors can request it.
prior authorization: Approval a plan requires before certain care. Denials for missing it can sometimes be reversed, especially for emergencies.
provider: Any doctor, hospital, lab, or clinic that gives you care.
self-funded: A job-based plan where your employer pays claims from its own money and hires an insurer only to administer it. State insurance laws generally do not apply; federal rules do.
Summary Plan Description: The booklet that describes your job-based plan's benefits and rules. It says whether the plan is self-funded.
utilization review: The process a plan uses to decide whether care is medically necessary, before, during, or after treatment.
